facts.text: The chestnut teal is a dabbling duck found in Australia and is protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974.
facts.quote: The chestnut teal (Anas castanea) is a dabbling duck found in Australia. It is protected under the National Parks and Wildlife Act 1974.

facts.text: The chestnut teal is darker and slightly bigger than the grey teal.
facts.quote: The chestnut teal is darker and a slightly bigger bird than the grey teal.

facts.text: The male has a distinctive green head and a mottled brown body, while the female has a brown head and mottled brown body.
facts.quote: The male has a distinctive green coloured head and mottled brown body. The female has a brown head and mottled brown body.

facts.text: The female has a loud penetrating "laughing" quack repeated rapidly nine times or more.
facts.quote: The female chestnut teal has a loud penetrating "laughing" quack repeated rapidly nine times or more.

facts.text: Chestnut teals form monogamous pairs that stay together outside the breeding season and defend the nest site.
facts.quote: Chestnut teals form monogamous pairs that stay together outside the breeding season, defend the nest site and look after the young when hatched.

facts.text: Nests are usually in a down-lined tree hollow about 6-10 m high over water, but sometimes on the ground among grass clumps near water.
facts.quote: Nests are usually located over water, in a down-lined tree hollow about 6–10 m (20–33 ft) high. Sometimes nests are placed on the ground, among clumps of grass near water.

facts.text: The young hatch and are ready to swim and walk within a day.
facts.quote: The young hatch and are ready to swim and walk within a day.

facts.text: It is common in south-eastern and south-western Australia, with Tasmania and southern Victoria its stronghold, and vagrants reaching New Guinea and New Zealand.
facts.quote: Tasmania and southern Victoria are the species' stronghold, while vagrants have been found as far north as New Guinea and Lord Howe Island, and as far south as New Zealand.

facts.text: It prefers coastal estuaries and wetlands, is indifferent to salinity, and eats both plant and animal food as an omnivore.
facts.quote: The chestnut teal prefers coastal estuaries and wetlands, and is indifferent to salinity. This bird is an omnivore.

facts.text: Its scientific name castanea comes from the Latin for "chestnut-coloured" or "chestnut-brown".
facts.quote: The specific epithet castanea is from the Latin castaneus for "chestnut-coloured" or "chestnut-brown".
